items.followUp: Differentiate between somatic cells and gametes.

rubric.why: Checks that somatic cells are identified as the non-reproductive cells of the body.
rubric.description: Identifies somatic cells as body cells other than reproductive cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that somatic cells make up the body and are not reproductive cells.

rubric.why: Checks the defining role of germ-line cells.
rubric.description: States that germ-line cells give rise to gametes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for saying that germ-line cells produce gametes.

modelAnswer: Somatic cells are the body cells other than the reproductive cells; they usually divide by mitosis.
Germ-line cells give rise to gametes, usually through meiosis.

items.followUp: Write two differences between mitosis and meiosis.

rubric.why: Checks the balanced reactants and products of the photosynthesis equation.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including the correct balanced reactants and products.

rubric.why: Checks that the conditions for photosynthesis are shown.
rubric.description: Shows that light and chlorophyll are required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including both sunlight and chlorophyll, such as over the reaction arrow.

items.followUp: What discovery is associated with the Calvin cycle?

rubric.why: Checks the year of the award.
rubric.description: Gives the year Calvin received the Nobel Prize.

rubric.why: Checks the reason for the award.
rubric.description: Relates the award to research on carbon dioxide assimilation in plants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying his research on carbon dioxide assimilation in plants.

modelAnswer: Melvin Calvin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1961.
He received it for his research on the assimilation of carbon dioxide in plants, which elucidated the Calvin cycle.

items.followUp: What is activation energy, and how does an enzyme affect it?

rubric.why: Checks how an enzyme helps the reaction proceed.
rubric.description: Explains that an enzyme binds substrates or provides an alternative pathway.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning enzyme–substrate complex formation, bringing substrates together, or an alternative pathway.

rubric.why: Checks the effect on the energy barrier.
rubric.description: States that the activation energy is reduced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explicitly stating that enzymes lower activation energy.

modelAnswer: An enzyme binds its substrate to form an enzyme–substrate complex and provides a pathway with a lower energy barrier.
Thus, less activation energy is needed for the reaction to occur.

items.followUp: Explain why an enzyme may stop working at a very high temperature.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of increasing temperature before the optimum is reached.
rubric.description: States that the rate increases as temperature rises up to the enzyme's optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the increase up to the optimum.

rubric.why: Checks the effect above the optimum temperature.
rubric.description: States that high temperature denatures the enzyme or alters its active site, reducing its activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking high temperature with denaturation or loss of activity.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of enzyme action increases up to the enzyme's optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature and its active site changes shape, so the rate decreases or stops.

items.followUp: How is the structure of the small intestine adapted for absorption?

rubric.why: Checks the identification and basic structure of villi.
rubric.description: Defines villi as finger-like projections in the lining of the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing their finger-like shape and location.

rubric.description: States that villi increase surface area and help absorb digested nutrients.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased surface area with absorption.

modelAnswer: Villi are tiny finger-like projections on the inner lining of the small intestine.
They increase the surface area and help absorb digested nutrients into the blood and lymph.

items.followUp: Trace the pathway of blood in pulmonary circulation.

rubric.why: Checks the direction of oxygenated blood from the heart to the body.
rubric.description: Traces blood from the left ventricle through the aorta to body tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct outward route.

rubric.why: Checks the return route of deoxygenated blood to the heart.
rubric.description: Traces blood from the body back through the venae cavae to the right atrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct return route.

modelAnswer: Systemic circulation carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta to the body tissues.
Deoxygenated blood returns from the body through the venae cavae to the right atrium.

items.followUp: Write a note on a dicotyledonous plant, giving its main identifying features.

rubric.why: Checks the general habit of mustard.
rubric.description: Identifies mustard as a herbaceous plant, commonly an annual.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mustard is an annual herb or herb.

rubric.description: Gives a dicot feature such as a taproot or reticulate leaf venation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either stated feature.

rubric.why: Checks a recognizable feature of mustard flowers.
rubric.description: Describes mustard's yellow flowers or their four petals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either stated feature.

rubric.why: Checks the fruit or seed characteristics of mustard.
rubric.description: Identifies its siliqua fruit or its oil-bearing seeds with two cotyledons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one accurate fruit or seed feature.

modelAnswer: Mustard is an annual herb and a dicotyledonous flowering plant.
It has a taproot and leaves with reticulate venation.
Its yellow flowers have four petals.
The fruit is a siliqua, and its oil-bearing seeds have two cotyledons.
